When traffic on the Harlow Road corridor grew intolerable, the regional council did what councils have done for a century: it added two lanes. For eighteen months the commute improved. Then, as later surveys showed, the improvement drew in people who had previously travelled at other hours, taken the train, or not made the trip at all. Within four years, peak travel times were back where they had started, and the corridor now carried thirty percent more cars.

Engineers call this induced demand, and it should not surprise anyone who has watched a free buffet. When the cost of something falls, people consume more of it. A faster road lowers the time cost of driving, so more people drive until the road is once again slow enough to discourage the marginal trip. The lesson is not that roads are useless; the wider corridor does move more people than the narrow one did. The lesson is that widening cannot, by itself, deliver the thing it is usually sold as delivering: a shorter commute.

If the council truly wants shorter commutes, it must change the price of the peak trip rather than the capacity of the road. A modest charge for driving the corridor between seven and nine in the morning would push some trips to other hours and other modes, and unlike new asphalt, it would not invite the very congestion it was meant to cure. Critics will call such a charge unfair to those with no alternative. They are right that it would need to be paired with better buses. They are wrong that the current arrangement is free: drivers already pay, in time.
prompt: Does the author argue that widening the corridor brought no benefit at all?
rationale: The author says the wider corridor does move more people; only the shorter-commute promise fails.

context:
Great tits living in cities sing differently from those in forests. Recordings from ten European city-forest pairs found that urban males consistently used a higher minimum frequency in their songs, while the maximum frequency changed little. The researchers' explanation was acoustic: traffic noise is concentrated at low frequencies, so a low note sung in a city is more likely to be masked. Raising the bottom of the song would keep more of it audible.

This explanation is attractive, but the recordings alone cannot establish it. City and forest differ in many ways besides noise. Buildings reflect sound differently from tree trunks; urban birds may be younger on average, or in different body condition; and the populations may have diverged genetically. Any of these could, in principle, shift song pitch.

A follow-up experiment addressed some of these doubts. Researchers played recorded traffic noise near the territories of individual forest birds and recorded them before, during and after playback. Many birds raised their minimum frequency during playback and lowered it again when the noise stopped. Because the same individuals were compared with themselves, differences in age, condition and ancestry could not explain the shift.

Even so, the experiment answers a narrower question than the first study raised. It shows that individual birds can adjust their songs to noise within minutes. It does not show that this flexibility, rather than inherited change, accounts for the whole difference between city and forest populations. Both may be at work.
prompt: According to the passage, does the design of the playback experiment rule out genetic differences as an explanation for the pitch shift it observed?
rationale: The same individuals were compared with themselves, so ancestry could not explain that shift.

context:
Every Thursday, Ines brought the clock back. It was a mantel clock in a walnut case, and every Thursday, Tomas found nothing wrong with it. He oiled the pivots she had watched him oil the week before, adjusted a beat that did not need adjusting, and wound it while she sat in the chair by the window with her handbag on her knees.

"It loses time," she said the first week. By the fifth week she had stopped giving reasons, and he had stopped asking for them. He charged her for the oil, which cost almost nothing, and once, when she insisted, for the labour, which he then returned to her as change for a note she had not handed him.

His apprentice, a quick boy who could already rebuild an escapement, watched this for a month and finally asked why they kept taking in a clock that kept perfect time.

Tomas held the clock to his ear a moment, as though the question might be answered in there. "It was her husband's," he said. "He wound it every Thursday night. Forty-one years." He set it down on the bench. "She doesn't bring it because it's broken."

The boy considered this. The following Thursday, when the bell over the door rang, he had already cleared the chair by the window and put the kettle on, and Tomas, seeing it, said nothing at all, which the boy understood was the highest praise he had ever received from him.
prompt: Does the passage suggest that Tomas found a way to avoid keeping Ines's payment for his labour?
rationale: He returned the labour charge as change for a note she had not handed him.

context:
Last year, Westbrook District moved its high schools to a four-day week, adding forty minutes to each remaining day. Attendance rose by four percentage points, and the district's average score on the state reading exam climbed from 61 to 66. The superintendent has called the results proof that a shorter week makes students learn more, and three neighbouring districts are now preparing to follow.

They should slow down. The same year Westbrook changed its calendar, it also hired eleven reading specialists with a state grant, and the state replaced a reading exam that many teachers considered confusing with a revised version. Either change could plausibly raise scores on its own. Attendance, meanwhile, is measured per scheduled day; a student who used to skip Fridays now looks perfectly regular simply because Fridays are no longer school days.

None of this means the four-day week failed. Teachers report that the longer days allow science labs to be finished in one sitting, and the district saved on bus fuel and heating. Those are real gains, and they may be worth having for their own sake. But a district considering the change in the hope of raising test scores has, at present, no good reason to expect it. What Westbrook offers is one year, one district and several simultaneous changes: an anecdote dressed as an experiment. If the neighbouring districts want to know whether the calendar helps, the most useful thing they could do is adopt it in some schools and not others, and compare.
prompt: Claim: the author concludes that the four-day week has harmed learning in Westbrook. Judge the claim against the passage.
rationale: The author says the change did not fail and has real gains; only the test-score claim is unsupported.

context:
When divers raised timbers from a wreck in the harbour mud, the first question was when the ship had been built. No cargo or coins survived to date it. The answer came instead from the wood.

Oak trees lay down one ring of growth each year, and the width of a ring depends on that year's weather: wide in mild, wet years, narrow in harsh ones. Because a whole region shares much the same weather, trees across it record the same pattern of wide and narrow rings. By overlapping the patterns from living trees, old buildings and buried timbers, researchers have built continuous reference sequences stretching back thousands of years. A sample with enough rings can be slid along the reference until its pattern matches, and each of its rings then receives a calendar year.

The wreck's planks matched the regional sequence well, and the outermost surviving ring on the best-preserved plank dated to 1612. That does not mean the tree was cut in 1612. Shipwrights trimmed planks, removing the soft outer sapwood and with it an unknown number of the final rings. Using the typical sapwood thickness for oaks of the region, the team estimated that the tree had been felled no earlier than 1622, and probably within a decade after that.

A further clue came from the pattern itself. Its closest match was not with local trees but with sequences from a forest some three hundred kilometres inland, suggesting the timber had been brought from there, a detail no written record had preserved.
prompt: Does the outermost surviving ring on the best-preserved plank give the year the tree was felled?
rationale: Sapwood and final rings were trimmed off, so felling was estimated as no earlier than 1622.
